summary: This document extends signature-based authentication in the Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2). IKEv2 had limited support for ECDSA, with only a few elliptic curve groups and a fixed hash algorithm tied to each. This standards-track update lets peers use a wider choice of signature and hash algorithms.

eli5.summary: Two computers prove who they are by signing messages, like signing a letter. This update lets them agree on more kinds of pens and ink, so they are not stuck with just a few.

questions: what is ikev2 digital signature authentication
subtitle: One IKEv2 authentication method that carries the signature algorithm with the signature, so new hashes and curves need no new codes.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 had a separate authentication method for each signature algorithm, and each ECDSA method was tied to one curve and one hash. Every new hash or curve would have needed yet another method.
tldr.mechanism: A new Digital Signature authentication method puts an ASN.1 AlgorithmIdentifier in front of the signature, and a SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS Notify payload tells the peer which hashes are supported.
tldr.outcome: IKEv2 can use any signature method that PKIX supports, including RSASSA-PSS, with the hash chosen from the other side's list. RFC 7427 updates RFC 7296 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 7427 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7296; the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IKEv2 Needed a Generic Signature Method
sections.content:
RFC 7427 adds a new authentication method to IKEv2 (RFC 7296). The existing signature methods are per algorithm: one for RSA, one for DSS using SHA-1, and three for different ECDSA curves, each tied to exactly one hash algorithm.

The RFC lists three problems with that design. RSA authentication uses RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 padding, although the newer RSASSA-PSS is now recommended. With ECDSA and DSS there is no way to extract the hash algorithm from the signature, so each new hash would need a new method; DSS was limited to SHA-1, which made long keys pointless. And tying ECDSA to particular curve groups means more methods for each new group, which the RFC says would become unmanageable.

The document therefore specifies two things: a new authentication method whose payload carries enough information to identify the signature hash algorithm, and a way to announce which hash algorithms each peer supports. There is no requirement to agree on one common hash, because different hashes can be used in each direction.
sections.eli5: Before, every kind of signature needed its own special rule, like a different form for every pen colour. Now there is one form with a box that says which pen was used.

sections.title: The Digital Signature Authentication Payload
sections.content:
The new Digital Signature method has Auth Method value 14. It works with any type of signature. Because IKEv2 authentication methods are not negotiated, a peer may use it only if the SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS Notify payload has been both sent and received. If both ends send and receive that Notify and signature authentication is used, this method MUST be used.

The Authentication Data field is laid out differently from other methods. It begins with a 1-octet ASN.1 Length, then the AlgorithmIdentifier ASN.1 object, then the signature value, with no padding between them. The object is the same AlgorithmIdentifier that PKIX uses (RFC 5280), encoded with DER. Its OID names both the signature algorithm and the hash. The length prefix lets simple implementations treat the object as a binary blob and compare it with a fixed set of known values, without parsing ASN.1.

Only RSASSA-PSS uses the optional parameters today; for others they are NULL or missing. Where an algorithm has two valid encodings, implementations SHOULD use the preferred one: with "preferredPresent" the parameters object is present (NULL if there are none), with "preferredAbsent" it is omitted. For hash truncation, the method in ANSI X9.62:2005 MUST be used.
sections.eli5: The signature now comes with a small label in front that says which kind of signature it is. The label has its own length written first, so even a simple computer can skip over it or compare it to a list.

sections.title: Announcing Supported Hash Algorithms
sections.content:
Each peer lists the hash algorithms it can use in a Notify payload of type SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS, sent inside the IKE_SA_INIT exchange. Sending it also implicitly says the peer supports the new Digital Signature method.

In that Notify the Protocol ID is 0, the SPI Size is 0 and the Notify Message Type is 16431. The notification data is a list of 16-bit hash algorithm identifiers taken from the IANA registry, with no padding between them.

When computing its signature, a peer MUST pick one algorithm that the other peer sent. The two directions can use different algorithms. The chosen hash and signature algorithm are then carried in the AlgorithmIdentifier inside the Authentication Data.
sections.eli5: Each side hands the other a list of the kinds of ink it can read. When signing, you pick one from the other side's list.

sections.title: Choosing the Public Key Type
sections.content:
The specification gives no way for peers to say which kinds of key pair they hold, so it describes ways a responder can work out what the initiator supports. One is for the initiator to signal the key it wants through the IDr payload in the IKE_AUTH request, when the responder has several identities that are each tied to a key or key type.

Another is the Certificate Request payload: if the initiator says it trusts a certificate authority certificate signed by an ECDSA key, the responder can safely use ECDSA keys. A third is for the responder to use the same key type the initiator used, which does not work when the initiator uses a shared secret or EAP.

If the initiator uses a key type the responder does not support, the responder replies with a Notify of error type AUTHENTICATION_FAILED. An initiator with several keys may then try another, and normally out-of-band configuration picks a key for each connection.
sections.eli5: The responder has to guess what kind of key the other side can handle. It can be told directly, can look at what the other side trusts, or can copy the kind of key the other side showed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the curve is no longer tied to a hash, different security levels can be mixed; the RFC's example is a 512-bit elliptic curve with SHA1. The security of the authentication is that of the weakest component (signature algorithm, hash algorithm or curve), which complicates analysis. Implementers may wish to add a way in the IKE policy databases to limit such mixing.

Downgrade attacks, where a man-in-the-middle removes or alters stronger methods, are not a significant concern in the AUTH payload, because a modified payload is detected when the peer computes a signature over the IKE messages. Attacks that need real-time breaking of weak ciphers should be blocked by policy on cipher selection.

MD5 is left out of the hash registry as not safe enough for signature use. The new method also removes two old limits: the known vulnerabilities of RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, and DSA being restricted to SHA-1.
sections.eli5: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. If you mix a very strong lock with a weak one, the weak one is what protects you.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
The RFC creates a new IANA registry for IKEv2 Hash Algorithms, changed by Expert Review. Values 5 to 1023 are unassigned, and 1024 to 65535 are reserved for Private Use among mutually consenting parties.

It also adds SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS (16431) to the IKEv2 Notify Message Types - Status Types registry and Digital Signature (14) to the IKEv2 Authentication Method registry. Appendix A gives the ASN.1 objects for commonly used algorithms as non-normative examples, and says the algorithm's own specification wins if they differ.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers gets a new page for hash types and two new entries, so everyone uses the same numbers.
